html:
Real neurons likely exceed the complexity of artificial/modeled neurons; one study claimed that a single pyramidal neuron is equivalent to a 5-8 layer, 1000-neuron ANN 1

Single neuron responses have helped us discover several key algorithms (e.g dopamine neurons for RL, grid cells for path integration) 2

Evolution of neuron models

Simple integrate-and-fire models, where membrane potential follows basic differential equations (τdV/dt=−V+RI(t)\tau dV/dt = -V + RI(t)), capture fundamental dynamics but miss the rich computational landscape of real neurons. 3 Some modern Hodgkin-Huxley based models incorporate ten or more ion channel types distributed across the soma, dendrites, and axon 4, while extensions can account for stochastic channel gating 5, temperature-dependent channel kinetics 6, and neuromodulatory changes in channel conductances 7. Differentiable simulators such as Jaxley can fit detailed neuron models to voltage and calcium recordings and train networks of these neurons to perform computational tasks 4. A 2025 study illustrates differentiable simulation of biophysically detailed neurons (Figure). The study also shows how a detailed neuron model can be fitted to voltage recordings (Figure).

Dendritic computation

Neurons receive thousands of synaptic inputs distributed across their dendritic tree. These dendrites do not merely funnel inputs to the soma; each dendritic branch can function as a semi-independent computational subunit.

Experiments and modeling have shown that tiny dendritic compartments can perform logical operations (e.g. acting as local AND/OR gates) on their incoming signals. 8, 9 In 2020, experiments on human cortical neurons and accompanying modeling showed that calcium-mediated dendritic action potentials could support an exclusive OR (XOR) operation - a function that a single linear-threshold artificial neuron cannot compute. 10 Experiments and models illustrate nonlinear integration in dendrites (Figure). The analysis relates dendritic nonlinearities to computable Boolean functions (Figure).

Dendritic spikes: two-photon glutamate-uncaging and in vivo voltage imaging show that when a small cluster of spines (typically 2-10 within  10 micrometers) co-activates within a  40 ms window, they ignite an NMDA-dependent calcium or plateau spike that lasts 50-300 ms and remains largely confined to that branch. The plateau acts as an eligibility trace: co-active synapses are potentiated, while nearby inactive synapses are heterosynaptically depressed, giving each branch an independent "credit-assignment" mechanism and allowing a single cortical pyramidal cell to store on the order of hundreds of distinct memories without catastrophic interference 11, 12 Experiments and modeling illustrate competition for shared resources among neighboring dendritic spines (Figure).

Heterogenous learning rules: recent in-vivo imaging during motor and sensory learning demonstrates that apical tufts, basal obliques, and trunk dendrites obey measurably different rules (STDP-like timing sensitivity at basal shafts versus rate-coincidence detection in the tuft), providing pathway-specific adaptation during behaviour 13.

Dendritic branches can also exhibit heterogeneous time constants ranging from 10-100ms, allowing neurons to operate across multiple timescales simultaneously. 14

The cutting edge of dendritic simulation lies in multi-compartmental models with 1000+ compartments, enabled by GPU acceleration and novel algorithms like Dendritic Hierarchical Scheduling that achieve 2-3 orders of magnitude speedup. 15 These models capture the full spatial complexity of dendritic trees, where voltage compartmentalization enables parallel processing across multiple branches. 8 A GPU simulation study illustrates the computational cost of detailed neuronal models (Figure). The paper explains its dendritic hierarchical scheduling algorithm (Figure).

As Gordon Shepherd put it, much of the brain’s processing is "actually subthreshold" within dendrites - a single neuron can operate as two or more layers of processing, theoretically able to compute almost any function if it has enough dendritic branches performing their own nonlinear operations. In essence, dendrites endow neurons with a kind of internal complexity that far exceeds the point-like neurons in typical artificial networks. Real neurons don’t just compute a weighted sum; they recognize complex spatiotemporal patterns across their dendrites.

This relates back to the recent work demonstrating that accurately simulating a single pyramidal neuron requires approximately 1,000 artificial neurons arranged in 5-8 layers. The study found that the source of this complexity is the neuron’s dendritic nonlinearities - especially NMDA receptor-dependent dendritic spikes. When NMDA channels (which can produce localized dendritic spikes) were removed from the neuron model, a much simpler network (only a single hidden layer) could approximate the neuron 1.

Temporal dynamics and filtering

Biological neurons are dynamic systems with internal states, meaning their output at any moment depends not just on instantaneous input, but also on the timing and history of inputs. 16

Different neurons exhibit different temporal integration characteristics. Some neurons behave primarily as integrators, summing inputs over relatively long windows; others act as coincidence detectors that require synchronous inputs in a narrow time window to fire. 17, 18

Which mode a neuron operates in can depend on its ion channels and the context. 18, 19 For example, under sparse firing conditions (when inputs are infrequent), a neuron tends to act like a coincidence detector - it may fire only if multiple inputs arrive coincidentally, since isolated inputs decay before summation. 20 In such cases the neuron is effectively detecting temporal correlations in its input. 17, 20 On the other hand, during sustained high-frequency input, neurons enter different regimes: the continual bombardment of synapses and the accumulation of afterhyperpolarization currents can make the neuron integrate inputs over longer periods or fire in a regular train.

Neurons also serve as filters of input patterns. Membrane ion channels (like IhI_{h} channels, K+K^+ channels, etc.) endow neurons with frequency-dependent responses: some neurons preferentially respond to low-frequency, steady inputs (acting as low-pass integrators), while others have resonant properties that make them respond most strongly to inputs at a particular frequency band (band-pass behavior). 21 For instance, certain neurons in the thalamus or cortex exhibit theta-frequency resonance, meaning they are especially responsive to rhythmic input around 5-10 Hz, due to specific channel dynamics. 21

In general, the rich internal dynamics (capacitive membranes, voltage-gated channels) allow neurons to perform a variety of temporal computations like delay integration, phase locking to oscillations, and selective sensitivity to input patterns over time. 16, 21

Diverse Firing Patterns

Neurons differ not only in morphology and connectivity but in their intrinsic firing patterns, meaning how they convert a given input current into a spike train. Classic intracellular recordings sorted neocortical neurons into regular-spiking, fast-spiking, and intrinsically bursting classes 22, 23, and later work added further types such as "chattering" pyramidal cells that fire high-frequency bursts at gamma rhythms 24. Large-scale standardized recordings now describe these patterns as continuous, multidimensional features that, combined with morphology and gene expression, define dozens of cell types in mouse cortex alone 25, 26. Recorded and modeled spike trains show how well simple models capture firing (Figure). The model comparison also distinguishes excitatory and inhibitory cells (Figure).

Much of this diversity comes from differences in the type and density of ion channels each cell expresses. For example, fast-spiking interneurons express Kv3 potassium channels, which repolarize the membrane quickly enough to allow sustained firing at hundreds of Hz 27. Simple two-variable models can reproduce more than 20 qualitatively distinct firing behaviors (tonic spiking, phasic spiking, adaptation, bursting, rebound spikes, resonance, bistability, etc.) by changing only a few parameters, so the repertoire is large even in reduced models 28, 29.

Spike-frequency adaptation: many neurons, including most cortical pyramidal cells, slow their firing over the course of a sustained input. Computationally, adaptation acts as a high-pass filter: it amplifies changes in the input and suppresses responses to constant input 30, 31. It also reduces correlations between successive responses to natural stimuli, removing temporal redundancy from the neural code 32. Neocortical pyramidal neurons adapt over several timescales at once, which can be described as fractional differentiation of the input. This lets a cell’s effective adaptation timescale follow the timescale of the stimulus rather than being fixed 33.

Bursting: other neurons fire bursts, i.e. brief clusters of spikes at high frequency. Because individual synapses transmit unreliably, a burst is more likely than a single spike to evoke a postsynaptic response, so bursts can act as a more reliable unit of information 34, 35. Thalamic relay neurons switch between tonic and burst modes depending on their membrane potential, which may let them alternate between faithfully relaying input and signalling the detection of a salient stimulus 36, 37. In layer 5 pyramidal neurons, bursts are produced when somatic and apical dendritic input coincide 38. This allows a single neuron to multiplex two signals: the rate of single spikes carries bottom-up information while the fraction of spikes occurring in bursts carries top-down information 39. Bursts are also important for plasticity; postsynaptic bursting is required for Hebbian LTP at hippocampal synapses 40, and models show that burst-dependent plasticity can approximate backpropagation-like credit assignment in hierarchical networks 41.

Persistent firing and bistability: some neurons keep firing after a transient input ends because of regenerative intrinsic currents. Layer V entorhinal neurons, under cholinergic modulation, show graded persistent firing in which each stimulus shifts the cell to a new stable firing rate that it holds for minutes. This is a single-cell mechanism that could support working memory or integration 42, 43. Likewise, calcium plateau potentials make motoneurons bistable, toggling between a quiescent state and a self-sustained firing state 44. These intrinsic mechanisms are distinct from, but complementary to, network-level persistent states such as cortical up-states, which arise mainly from recurrent excitation balanced by inhibition 45, 46.

Firing patterns are not fixed properties of a cell type. Neuromodulators change ion channel conductances and can move a single neuron between tonic, bursting, and silent modes on behavioral timescales 47, and similar firing behavior can arise from very different combinations of channel densities 48, 49.

Why diversity may matter computationally: diversity in intrinsic properties decorrelates the responses of neurons that receive the same input and increases the information a population carries 50. In spiking neural networks trained with gradient descent, letting membrane time constants vary across neurons improves learning and robustness on temporal tasks 51. When networks can also learn conduction delays, time constants, and bursting, an adjustable bursting parameter was essential for solving the more complex spatio-temporal tasks 52. Together these results suggest that the variety of single-neuron dynamics is a computational resource rather than biological noise, and that ANNs built from identical units without internal state give up a set of useful temporal filters, memory mechanisms, and gating signals. A computational study investigates how neuron time constants support different tasks (Figure). The study also examines how its solutions behave with noisy inputs and parameters (Figure).

Energy efficiency

The human brain is about 2% of body mass but uses roughly 20% of the body’s resting energy, about 20 W 53. Most of this budget pays for signaling, i.e. for pumping back the ions that move during action potentials and synaptic currents. In cortical grey matter, synaptic transmission is the largest single cost 54, 55, 56. One recent estimate divides cortical energy use into about 0.1 W for computation (synaptic integration and dendritic processing) and about 3.5 W for communication (sending action potentials along axons), so moving information costs far more than processing it 57.

Comparisons with digital hardware are often made but are imprecise. The human neocortex contains on the order of 101410^{14} synapses 58, and with mean firing rates below a few Hz this gives very roughly 101310^{13}–101510^{15} synaptic events per second. A synaptic event is not a floating-point operation, though: it is analog, noisy, and fails often, so the "exascale at 20 W" comparison with supercomputers such as Frontier (about 1 exaFLOP/s at about 20 MW 59) should be taken as illustrating the scale of the gap, not as an equivalence.

Energy constrains coding: because each spike is expensive, energy limits how many neurons can be strongly active at once. Estimates suggest that only a small fraction of cortical neurons (possibly under 1%) can be substantially active at the same time, with mean cortical firing rates well below 1 Hz 60, 61. Theoretical work shows that once energy is counted, the code that maximizes information per unit energy uses low firing rates and sparse activity, not the code that maximizes information alone 62, 63. This fits the sparse codes seen in sensory cortex 64.

Energy-saving mechanisms at the single-cell level: several features of neurons look like adaptations for saving energy. Some axons time their sodium and potassium currents so that there is little overlap between them, bringing ion flux close to the theoretical minimum for an action potential 65. How efficient action potentials are varies across neuron types, which reflects trade-offs between speed and cost 66. Synapses that release transmitter only part of the time also save energy while keeping most of the information they carry 67, 68. At the circuit level, cortical wiring appears to keep wire length short, limiting the cost of communication 69, 70.

Energy budgets are adjusted by need: cortex can trade precision for energy. In food-restricted mice, layer 2/3 neurons in visual cortex reduce the ATP they spend on synaptic currents by about 29% while keeping their firing rates the same. The cost is broader orientation tuning and worse fine visual discrimination, and this trade-off is signaled by the hormone leptin 71. So efficiency is not a fixed design point but a control variable that the brain adjusts to metabolic state. The loss of fine visual discrimination makes this energy–precision tradeoff visible (Figure).

For artificial systems, the lesson is that the brain’s efficiency comes mostly from not computing. It does this through sparse, event-driven activity, local computation that avoids long-distance communication, and accepting noise where precision is not needed. Dense, synchronous, high-precision operations, as in most ANNs, run against all three, which is one reason conditional computation (e.g. mixture-of-experts), activation sparsity, low-precision arithmetic, and event-driven neuromorphic hardware are being explored.

Noise and variability

Neurons are unreliable devices. Repeating the same stimulus produces different spike trains on each trial, and noise enters at every stage: in sensory transduction, in the random opening and closing of ion channels, in synaptic release, and in the variable timing of spike generation 72, 73. ANN units are deterministic by contrast (apart from noise added deliberately during training), so variability is one of the clearest differences between the two.

Sources at the cellular level: at many central synapses a presynaptic spike releases a vesicle only part of the time, with release probabilities often well below 0.5 74, 75. Ion channel noise matters most in small structures. Simulations suggest that unmyelinated axons thinner than about 0.1–0.2 μ\mum would fire spontaneous action potentials from channel noise alone, which sets a lower limit on how thin the brain’s wiring can be 76. Spike generation itself is fairly precise: a cortical neuron given the same fluctuating current fires with millisecond-reproducible timing across trials, while constant current gives jittered timing 77. This suggests much of the variability seen in vivo comes from the network rather than from the neuron.

Sources at the network level: cortical neurons in vivo fire irregularly, roughly like a Poisson process 78, 79. This is expected in networks where large excitatory and inhibitory inputs nearly cancel, leaving membrane potential to be driven by fluctuations 80. Much of the apparent "noise" is in fact ongoing activity that the experimenter does not control. The state of ongoing activity at stimulus onset accounts for a large part of the trial-to-trial variability in evoked responses 81, and in mice much of it likely reflects the animal’s own spontaneous movements, which are represented throughout the brain 82, 83. Variability is also state-dependent: stimulus onset reduces it across many cortical areas 84, and attention improves performance largely by reducing correlated variability between neurons 85.

Variability as a resource:

Representing uncertainty. Under the sampling hypothesis, the variability of neural responses reflects samples from the brain’s posterior beliefs about the world, so the spread of responses represents uncertainty 86, 87. A sampling-based model of V1 accounts for several features of its response variability and correlations 88. As animals mature, spontaneous activity in ferret V1 becomes more similar to stimulus-evoked activity averaged over natural scenes, which is what an internal model adapted to the environment predicts 89. A different proposal, probabilistic population codes, holds that Poisson-like variability lets populations represent uncertainty implicitly and makes Bayesian cue combination simple to compute 90.

Exploration. In songbirds, a basal ganglia-forebrain circuit actively injects variability into song, and this variability is needed for vocal learning 91, 92. In humans, people with more task-relevant motor variability learn faster, and training reshapes that variability to fit the task 93, 94. This is the biological counterpart of exploration noise in reinforcement learning.

Detection and learning. Moderate noise can make weak, subthreshold signals detectable (stochastic resonance), although its importance in vivo is still debated 95. Treating synaptic weights as fluctuating samples rather than fixed values lets networks represent uncertainty about their own parameters and keep adapting, which is closely related to Bayesian neural networks and to dropout in deep learning 96, 97, 98.

Variability also unfolds over days. Single-neuron tuning in hippocampus and parietal cortex drifts over days to weeks while behavior stays stable 99, 100. This raises the question of how downstream readouts stay consistent with a changing code 101.

Mixed selectivity

The traditional picture of neural coding is one of specialization, with each neuron tuned to one feature such as an orientation, a place, or a face. Some regions do fit this picture well, for example face patches in macaque temporal cortex where nearly all cells are face-selective 102. In higher association areas, however, most neurons respond to combinations of task variables (stimulus identity, rule, context, upcoming action) that are hard to label. This is called mixed selectivity 103, 104. A 2026 recurrent-network study shows learned stimulus and mismatch representations (Figure) 120.

Linear versus nonlinear mixing: if a neuron’s response is a weighted sum of its selectivities to individual variables, the mixing is linear and adds little. The computational value comes from nonlinear mixed selectivity, where the response to a combination of variables differs from the sum of responses to each. Recording from monkey prefrontal cortex during a sequence memory task, Rigotti and colleagues found that nonlinear mixed selectivity was common, that every task variable could be decoded from the population even when individual cells were not selective for it, and that the dimensionality of the population’s representation collapsed on error trials, linking high dimensionality to correct behavior 103. The study also compares mixed stimulus and error representations in model and mouse cortex (Figure).

Why it helps: a population with nonlinear mixed selectivity represents task conditions in a high-dimensional space, and in a high-dimensional space many more input–output mappings can be implemented with a simple linear readout 105. This lets downstream neurons learn many different context-dependent rules from the same population without rewiring it 104. The same principle underlies random-feature and kernel methods in machine learning 106 and the large expansion layer of cerebellar granule cells, where sparse, mixed inputs maximize the number of patterns that can be separated 107, 108. Sparseness controls a trade-off, since denser mixing improves discrimination between conditions while sparser mixing improves generalization 109.

Mixed selectivity in other areas and how it arises: mixed or "category-free" responses are also found in posterior parietal cortex during decision-making 110 and in medial entorhinal cortex, where many cells combine position, head direction, and speed 111. Prefrontal populations can select and integrate context-relevant inputs through recurrent dynamics even though single neurons mix all task variables 112, and mixed selectivity in prefrontal cortex can reorganize as task demands change 113. Random connectivity combined with simple Hebbian learning is enough to reproduce the selectivity statistics seen in prefrontal cortex, so mixed selectivity does not require a special wiring rule 114.

Specialization and mixing coexist: mixed selectivity is not the same as unstructured coding. In rat orbitofrontal cortex, neurons fall into distinct functional types that each encode a single decision variable such as confidence or reward value, which argues against purely random mixing 115. At the population level, hippocampal and prefrontal representations can be both high-dimensional and abstract. Some variables are encoded along consistent directions, which allows linear decoders trained in one condition to generalize to new ones 116, and such abstract structure emerges naturally in networks trained on many tasks 117. A better answer to "is specialization the exception?" is that the brain balances high dimensionality, for flexibility, against abstract, low-dimensional structure, for generalization, and that the balance differs across regions.

Mixed selectivity in brains resembles polysemanticity in ANNs, where single units respond to several unrelated features, possibly because networks store more features than they have units ("superposition") 118, 119. In both cases, the meaningful unit of analysis is often the population and its geometry rather than the single neuron.
